Arctic ground squirrels breeding in the Alaskan interior exhibit a tightly constrained annual cycle shaped by the extreme seasonality of their environment. Following emergence from hibernation, females must quickly initiate parturition to allow sufficient time for offspring development before the next winter. Gestation is relatively brief, lasting approximately 27 days [tg = approximately 27 days] during the active season at a body temperature of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C], a duration consistent with that observed in other sciurid rodents of comparable body size. The litter size at birth shows considerable variation, with reported fecundity ranging from six pups per litter [N_R_i = six pups per litter], and the maximum reproductive rate is achieved when females successfully wean a single large litter annually [F_R_i = single large litter annually], reflecting the brief window of resource abundance available during the short arctic summer.

Neonatal Arctic ground squirrels emerge from the birth canal weighing a mere 13.9 grams [Wwb = 13.9 grams], an initial body mass that places them among the smaller relative birth sizes observed in the genus. This altricial state necessitates an extended period of intense maternal investment through lactation. The nursing offspring remain entirely dependent on milk for their early development, with the suckling juvenile phase culminating in nutritional independence at weaning. The time since birth at weaning is typically 35 days since birth [tx = 35 days since birth] at the active body temperature of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C], a value that falls within the reported range of 28 to 35 days since birth (28-35 days since birth) [tx = 28-35 days since birth] for this species. By the time of provisioning cessation, the weaned offspring have attained a substantial proportion of adult mass, with wet weight at weaning recorded at 199 grams [Wwx = 199 grams]. This marked increase over the course of just over one month reveals a rapid growth trajectory fueled by the high energetic content of maternal milk.

As juveniles transition to independent foraging, they undergo a prolonged period of somatic development before attaining sexual maturation. The time since birth at puberty is approximately 200 days since birth [tp = approximately 200 days since birth] at the typical active body temperature of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C], meaning that individuals born during the early summer months will only reach reproductive maturity during the following calendar year. This delay in the onset of gonadal activity is characteristic of hibernating sciurids, where the first winter hibernation typically occurs before the initiation of reproductive effort. The ultimate wet weight achieved by adults of this species shows significant sexual dimorphism. While females generally attain a maximum adult body mass of 750 grams [Wwi = 750 grams], adult males are considerably larger and can reach an ultimate wet weight of 850 grams [Wwi = 850 grams], a difference that likely reflects selective pressures related to male-male competition during the brief breeding season.

The resting metabolic rate of the Arctic ground squirrel, measured during the active season, provides a window into the energetic machinery supporting its high-latitude lifestyle. Basal oxygen consumption in post-absorptive, resting adults is maintained at 400.2 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 400.2 milliliters of oxygen per hour] when measured at a body temperature of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C]. This metabolic expenditure is relatively elevated for a mammal of this body size, a necessity for sustaining the physiological processes required during the brief arctic summer when food must be consumed and fat reserves accumulated for the prolonged hibernation period. The metabolic cost of thermoregulation is partly offset by the species' remarkable ability to withstand hypothermia during torpor, yet during the active phase, maintaining a body temperature near 35.5 °C is critical for normal enzymatic function and digestive efficiency.

Longevity records for free-living Arctic ground squirrels indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 8.3 years [am = approximately 8.3 years] at the active body temperature regime of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C], a remarkable achievement for a rodent of its size occupying such a demanding environment. This extended survival is facilitated by the safety of the hibernation period, which reduces exposure to predation and the energetic costs of winter foraging. The life history strategy of this species is thus characterized by a trade-off: relatively short active seasons constrain annual reproductive output, but the resulting high annual survival rates during hibernation allow individuals to accumulate multiple reproductive attempts over a lifespan that is long compared to many temperate-zone ground squirrels. Field studies continue to refine these demographic parameters, integrating data from long-term mark-recapture programs to better understand how climate change may alter the intricate phenological synchronization between reproduction, hibernation emergence, and the pulsed availability of arctic forage. The interplay between environmental constraints and physiological adaptations has made this species a model organism for studying mammalian responses to seasonal extremes, particularly given its ability to survive extended periods of fasting while maintaining minimal metabolic expenditure.
